analysis.one_liner: Requires farm equipment makers to share repair manuals, parts, software, and tools with owners and independent shops.
analysis.headline: The Agricultural Right to Repair Act was introduced in September 2023 with 9 cosponsors, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and never received a markup, a vote, or floor action before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Farm equipment today is heavily computerized, and manufacturers like John Deere control the software, diagnostic tools, and parts needed to fix it. This bill would require manufacturers to make repair documentation, parts, software, and tools available to equipment owners and independent repair shops on fair terms — manuals and software free of charge, tools at no cost to farmers, and parts without pairing locks that block third-party repairs. It would also let owners get the data their own machines generate and override copyright law that currently blocks repair work. The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the rules. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Farmers and ranchers who own or lease tractors, combines, and sprayers. Today a breakdown during planting or harvest can mean waiting days or weeks for a licensed dealer's technician; the bill would let owners and local independent mechanics fix machines themselves using the same manuals, tools, and parts the dealer network gets. Independent agricultural repair shops would gain access to the diagnostic software and parts they are currently locked out of, and the FTC would have a new enforcement tool against manufacturers that refuse.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Farmers and independent equipment repair shops

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires original equipment manufacturers to make documentation, parts, software, firmware, and repair tools available to any owner or independent repair provider on fair and reasonable terms [S2].
Documentation must be free (except printing and postage costs for physical copies), and tools must be free for farmers and priced no higher for independent shops than for authorized dealers [S2].
The bill bars manufacturers from requiring that parts be registered, paired, or approved before they work, and prohibits imposing conditions designed to impede independent repair [S2].
Owners would get access to the data their own equipment generates, and to the tools needed to disable electronic security locks on their machines [S2].

The bill overrides section 1201 of the Copyright Act so that circumventing software locks for diagnosis, maintenance, repair, interoperability, or security research is lawful, and it places OEM documentation, parts, software, or tools in the public domain if the OEM stops offering them to its own dealer network [S2].
Violations would be enforced by the Federal Trade Commission as unfair or deceptive acts or practices, with FTC rulemaking authority to implement the requirements [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Farm equipment manufacturers. They would lose their near-monopoly over post-sale repair: dealer service departments and OEM-priced parts are a major, high-margin revenue stream, and the bill would open that market to owners and independent shops at dealer-equivalent or free pricing. Equipment prices at purchase could also shift upward if manufacturers lose repair revenue.
analysis.who_pays_short: Farm equipment manufacturers and their dealer networks

drawbacks.text: The bill limits but does not eliminate safety and environmental risks: it explicitly bars disabling safety notification systems, escaping emissions compliance, or other illegal modifications, but critics of right-to-repair laws argue that wider access to calibration and programming tools makes emissions tampering and unsafe modifications harder to police [S2].

Manufacturers argue their software, diagnostics, and engineering documentation are proprietary intellectual property built at significant cost, and that forced disclosure risks exposing trade secrets — the bill addresses this by protecting trade secrets except where needed to supply repair materials, but a good-faith objection remains [S2].

Shifting service work away from trained dealer networks could raise questions about repair quality on complex, high-horsepower machines, and any lost service revenue could be recovered through higher new-equipment prices for farmers [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and concentrated on a group with real urgency: a combine that sits idle during a two-week harvest window costs a farmer far more than the repair itself, and manufacturer-controlled repair is a widely documented source of downtime and expense. The bill was drafted with notable care about the strongest objections — it protects trade secrets, preserves emissions and safety rules, and only overrides copyright where repair is the purpose. The main honest cost is to manufacturers' service profits, which is precisely the point of the bill. On balance the design addresses its likely downsides, and the chief reason it failed was not its content but that it never moved in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which sent it to a subcommittee, and it sat there until the Congress ended with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez introduced the Agricultural Right to Repair Act on September 20, 2023 [S1].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on September 20, 2023, and on September 22, 2023 was referred further to the Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce [S4].
Nine House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did [S3].

No further action appears in the bill's action history: there was no subcommittee hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote, and no Senate companion action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Farm equipment manufacturers are better off because the bill died: they keep exclusive control of diagnostic software, repair tools, parts pairing, and dealer service revenue for their machines. Farmers and independent repair shops remain in the same position as before, dependent on authorized dealers for repairs.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 sponsors — the sponsor and 9 cosponsors — were House Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-led Energy and Commerce Committee took no action on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would strip OEMs of their lock on repair: they would have to give away documentation and tools, sell parts on dealer-equivalent terms, and stop using software pairing to block independent fixes. Post-sale service and parts are a major profit center for these companies, which is why their interest runs against the farmers the bill serves.
The bill would give these shops access to the manuals, diagnostic software, and un-paired parts they are currently denied, letting them compete for repair work they are largely locked out of today.
Owners could fix their own machines, use their own equipment data, and avoid dealer wait times and OEM-only parts pricing — the direct beneficiaries of the bill.
Dealers would lose some captive service and parts revenue to owners and independent shops, but the bill preserves their arrangements with OEMs and lets them benefit from the same fair-terms access.
